text:
Date Released:  June 23, 1994                      No.
SO17205

New
Westminster Registry

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF
BRITISH COLUMBIA

BETWEEN:                       )

)

GORDON S. WATSON          )       REASONS
FOR JUDGMENT

)

PETITIONER  )

)
OF THE HONOURABLE

)

AND:                           )

)
MR. JUSTICE SHAW

CITY OF BURNABY           )

)

RESPONDENT  )

Counsel for the petitioner:    Mr.
Watson appeared for himself

Counsel for the respondent:               Ms.
M.M.T. MacKinnon

Place and dates of trial:                New
Westminster, B.C.

May
9 and 10, 1994

On March 14, 1994 the City of
Burnaby approved a request by The Gavel Historical Society to construct a
replica of a 1914 Masonic Lodge on city lands at the Burnaby Village Museum.
The approval was given by way of a resolution of the Burnaby City Council.

The petitioner, Gordon J. Watson,
is a resident of Burnaby.  He is opposed to the re-creation of the former
Masonic Lodge.  He petitions the court to set aside the resolution.

Mr. Watson's petition sets out
eleven grounds, all written in lay language.  He further elucidated his case by
oral submissions.  I have endeavoured to distill from his petition and his
submissions the arguable grounds.  They are as follows:

1
.   The resolution involves the
expenditure of public money to support a religion and this is not authorized by
the
Municipal Act
, R.S.B.C. 1979, c.290.

2
.   The resolution violates the
guarantee of freedom of religion set out in s-
s.2(a)
of the
Canadian Charter
of Rights and Freedoms
.

3
.   The resolution violates the right
of equal benefit under the law without discrimination based upon religion,
which right is set out in s-
s.15(1)
of the
Charter
.

4
.   One of the councillors who voted
on the resolution is a Mason and was therefore in a conflict of interest
position and had an appearance of bias.

5
.   One of the opponents to the
resolution was told by the City Clerk that he would advise her when the
resolution was to be voted upon and he failed to do so.

Mr. Watson contends that Masonry
is a religion.  The first three of the above grounds (and perhaps the fourth)
are based upon this premise.  Mr. Watson put in evidence several publications
which set out conflicting views on whether Masonry is a religion.  These
publications include "The Facts on The Masonic Lodge" by John
Ankerberg and John Weldon, "Masonry - Beyond the Light" by William

Schnoebelen, an article in The
Christian Research Journal, Winter 1994, entitled "The Masonic Lodge and
The Christian Conscience" authored by John Weldon, and "The Masonic
Report" by C.F. McQuaig and James D. Shaw.

In my view it is not necessary to
render a decision on the debate of whether Masonry is a religion.  I say so
because even if Masonry is considered a religion, that will make no difference
to the outcome of this case.  I will expand on this as I address the various
grounds based upon religion.

The resolution of the Burnaby
City Council reads:

"That
the recommendations of the City Manager be adopted."

The recommendations of the City
Manager referred to in the resolution are as follows:

"
RECOMMENDATIONS
:

1.THAT
the request of the Gavel Society to build a 1914 Heritage Masonic Lodge
Building at Burnaby Village Museum be approved subject to the signing of the
requisite agreements.

2.THAT
the legal agreement to cover the construction and the operation of the building
be prepared for Commission and Council approval."

The recommendations are contained
in a report by the City Manager to the City Council.  The report concerns a
proposal by The Gavel Historical Society to build a replica Heritage Masonic
Lodge.  The report states that the building is to be a copy of the Masonic
Lodge that was built in 1914 at the corner of Boundary Road and Kingsway.  The
1914 building was Burnaby's first Masonic Lodge.  The replica will be located
at the Burnaby Village Museum on a lane just off Village Street.  The
construction will be paid for by The Gavel Historical Society at an estimated
cost of $600,000.  The land is owned by the City of Burnaby and is valued at
approximately $400,000.  The City will become the owner of the building and
will have control thereof.  The City and the Society will share the maintenance
expense during the first two years, after which the cost will be taken over by
the City.  The estimated cost is $38,000 per year.

I will address each of the five
principle grounds that I set out earlier.

1.
Is the resolution authorized
by the Municipal Act?

I will deal with this point on
the basis of the provisions of the
Municipal Act
without reference to
the
Charter
arguments.  These will be dealt with later.

Burnaby's position is that the
replica lodge will be essentially a museum and that such an undertaking is
specifically authorized by the
Municipal Act
.  Burnaby relies upon the
following provisions:

679.
(1) The council may by bylaw

(a)acquire,
accept and hold any property in the municipality for pleasure, recreation or
community uses of the public, including public library, art gallery,
museum
,
arena and exhibition buildings;

(b)make
rules and regulations governing the management, maintenance, improvement,
operation, control and use of property mentioned in paragraph (a);

(c)lease
or rent property mentioned in paragraph (a) and owned or held by the
municipality;

(emphasis
added)

682.
(1)The council may, on property acquired or held, construct, maintain, operate,
improve and use buildings and other improvements and provide accommodation,
facilities or equipment requisite for any purpose mentioned in section
679(1)(a);

223. Unless
expressly required to be exercised by bylaw, all powers of a council may be
exercised by bylaw or by resolution.

287. The
council, in addition to powers specifically allotted to it, has power to do
anything incidental or conducive to the exercise of an allotted power.

I observe that the above
provisions authorize Burnaby to acquire and hold property for museum purposes;
construct and maintain buildings for museum purposes; do things which are
incidental or conducive to the exercise of its powers; and exercise its powers
by resolution except where expressly required to do so by by-law.

What is the essential purpose of
the replica lodge?  In my opinion the purpose is evident from the City
Manager's report.  It indicates that the nature of the proposed building will
be historical and that it will be an integral part of the Burnaby Village
Museum.  I refer to the following excerpts from the report:

"
SUMMARY
:

Construction
is recommended of a facsimile Heritage Masonic Lodge building at Burnaby
Village Museum at no capital cost to the City which will provide:

(a)a
facsimile Burnaby heritage building to place in a lane just off the Museum
"Village Street:"

(b)full
public ownership by the City;

(c)public
use of and public access to all segments of the building;

(d)historic
living and static displays to enhance the Museum experience; plus

(e)approximately
1,500 sq. ft. of prime space for Burnaby's use as a traditional Burnaby
storyline Museum with an opportunity to display Burnaby's archives, heritage
materials, etc. plus

(f)approximately
1,500 sq. ft. of second floor space for use by school children or for public
rentals or for public programming;

(g)possibly
in excess of 3,000 sq. ft. of basement space for storage and ancillary Museum
uses."

"
PRECEDENTS
IN OTHER LOCATIONS
:

The
inclusion of a facsimile masonic building in living museums is common in
Canada. Precedents exist in Fort Edmonton, Calgary Heritage Park, Black Creek
Village in Toronto, Barkerville, (B.C. Provincial Government) and one is
currently under construction at Fort Steele (Federal Government). It is often
provided at the expense of a local society similar to the Gavel Society."

"
THE
SUITABILITY OF BURNABY VILLAGE MUSEUM AS THE PROPOSED SITE
:

The
Museum's mandate is 1892-1925. The proposed building (1914) falls within this
time period. It occupied a prominent location at the corner of Boundary and
Kingsway and fits within the combination of real and facsimile buildings which
have been erected at the Museum. It does not interfere with the current Master
Plan for Museum development."

In this case Burnaby acted by way
of resolution, not by by-law.  The resolution approves the building of the
replica lodge subject to the signing of the requisite agreements which are to
be prepared for the approval of the Burnaby City Council and the Burnaby Parks
and Recreation Commission.  In my view the approval of the resolution is
"incidental or conducive" to the exercise of the power to construct,
maintain and operate a museum.  There is no requirement that this step be by
way of by-law.  It may therefore be done by resolution.

Mr. Watson contends that the
building will be used for religious purposes.  To support this contention he
refers to a document entitled "Points for Consideration for Inclusion in
Agreements between the City and the Society".  This document forms part of
the City Manager's report.  Specifically, Mr. Watson relies upon paragraphs
3(a), (c) and 9 under the heading "Daily Control/Opening
Hours/Etc.".  I will quote all the paragraphs (1 through 9) so the
portions relied upon by Mr. Watson can be read in context:

"
DAILY
CONTROL/OPENING HOURS/ETC.

1.City
controls keys and access. Society secures book room.

2.Public
open hours will be as per Museum hours.

3.Society
will be granted reasonable out of hours access.

a)for
artifacts, exhibits, and book room review and work

b)for
general purpose room rental

c)for
lodge room rental

d)for
viewing by visitors

e)all
above occasions by prior arrangement

f)facility
not for use as a Society "Clubroom" or as regular meeting space.

4.Agreement
for cost or noncharge uses by Society as per #3 above to be mutually agreed.

5.Daily
interface to be between one Society appointee and one City appointee.

6
.Consideration
to be given to creating a committee of City and Society representatives for
discussion of any emerging concerns.

7
.Use
of artifacts and exhibits arrived at by mutual cooperation with the quality of
artifacts and exhibits to be the subject of review and consent by the City.

8
.Volunteers
from the Society will be asked to assume a general Museum perspective; abide by
rules and regulations of Museum; take advantage of Museum orientation training
sessions, and preferably to dress in period.

9
.Agreed
there will be no pro-active promotional or recruiting activities for Masonic
membership or support but information material will be available indicating
what the Lodge is and what the Masons are. Questions answered by
volunteers."

Mr. Watson submits that because
The Gavel Historical Society can use the premises for "work"
(pursuant to sub-para.3(a)) this use will be for religious purposes.  He
further contends that if the Lodge can be rented (sub-para.3(c)) it will be
used for religious purposes.  He submits as well that if volunteers can answer
questions and provide informational material on what the Lodge is and what the
Masons are (paragraph 9), the volunteers will use these means to spread the
religious beliefs of the Masons.

As an initial observation, I note
that the above listed nine paragraphs are "Points for Consideration for
Inclusion in Agreements".  They are not written in stone.  I observe as
well that the provisions relied upon by Mr. Watson must be read in context.
Some of the context is provided by the opening words of paragraph 9 which
prohibit "pro-active promotional or recruiting activities for Masonic
membership or support".  Further context is provided by sub-paragraph 3(f)
which says that the facility is not to be used as a clubroom or regular meeting
place for the Society.  In my view, nothing in sub-paragraphs 3(a) and (c) when
read in context supports an inference that the "work" or the
"rental" will be for religious purposes.  Nor in my opinion does
paragraph 9 support the inference that the replica lodge will be used to do
what the opening words of paragraph 9 expressly forbid.

As I found earlier, Burnaby has
the authority under the
Municipal Act
to use its property for the
purpose of a museum.  It has the authority to construct, maintain and use
buildings on its property for museums and it has the power to do anything
incidental or conducive to the exercise of its powers.  In my opinion the
resolution is a valid exercise of these powers.

For the above reasons I find
against Mr. Watson on the first ground.

2.
Freedom of religion

Mr. Watson contends that the
resolution violates his right to freedom of religion.  This right is provided
for in s-
s.2(a)
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
:

2.Everyone
has the following fundamental freedoms:

(a)freedom
of conscience and religion;

Freedom of religion has been
defined by the Supreme Court of Canada in
R.
v.
Big M Drug Mart Ltd.
,

1985 CanLII 69 (SCC)
,
[1985] 1 S.C.R. 295
and
in
Jones
v.
The Queen
,
1986 CanLII 32 (SCC)
,
[1986] 2 S.C.R.
284
at 310-11
.  In the latter case, Wilson J., writing for the majority on this
point, said:

"The
core of this freedom was identified by Dickson J. (now C.J.)
in
R. v. Big M
Drug Mart Ltd.
,
1985 CanLII 69 (SCC)
,
[1985] 1 S.C.R. 295
at p.336
:

The
essence of the concept of freedom of religion is the right to entertain such
religious beliefs as a person chooses, the right to declare religious beliefs
openly and without fear of hindrance or reprisal, and the right to manifest
religious belief by worship and practice or by teaching and
dissemination."

In my opinion the resolution does
not constitute a direct violation of Mr. Watson's or anybody else's freedom of
religion.  It in no way prevents or hinders any person from openly holding and
practising his or her religious beliefs.

However, the nub of Mr. Watson's
submission is that the resolution has an indirect effect on his freedom of
religion by the devotion of tax dollars to support a religion not his own.

In
Jones
v.
The Queen

(supra) the Supreme Court of Canada dealt with an argument that there may be a
violation of
s.2
(a) by the "effects" of legislation as distinct from
its "purpose".  Wilson J., after holding that the real purpose of the
legislation in question was "to ensure that children receive an adequate
education", went on to address the "effects" argument.  Writing
for the majority on this point, she said, at pp.313-4:

"The
appellant's real complaint, it seems to me, is effects-based rather than
purpose-based. It is the effect of the statutory machinery for certification on
his religious beliefs that he is concerned about and he points to this Court's

decision in
R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.
, supra,
at p.331 as authority for
the proposition that legislation may be invalidated if its effect is to violate
a constitutional guarantee. However, even assuming that this legislation does
affect the appellant's beliefs, which for the reasons given I doubt, not every
effect of legislation on religious beliefs or practices is offensive to the
constitutional guarantee of freedom of religion.
Section 2
(a) does not require
the legislature to refrain from imposing any burdens on the practice of
religion. Legislative or administrative action whose effect on religion is
trivial or insubstantial is not, in my view, a breach of freedom of religion. I
believe that this conclusion necessarily follows from the adoption of an
effects-based approach to the
Charter
."

further, at p.314:

"To
state that any legislation which has an effect on religion, no matter how
minimal, violates the religious guarantee "would radically restrict the
operating latitude of the legislature"."

and at p.315:

"In
my view, the appellant has failed to show any substantial impact of this legislation
on his belief that God and not the state is the true source of authority over
the education of his children."

In the present case the true
purpose of the resolution is to provide a museum relating to an aspect of the
history of Burnaby.  The resolution is not for the purpose of promoting or
supporting a religion.  In my view the proposed replica lodge building and its
attendant call upon the public purse will have no effect of substance on
anyone's freedom of religion.

For the above reasons I hold that
the resolution of the Burnaby Council does not violate Mr. Watson's freedom of
religion guaranteed by s-
s.2(a)
of the
Charter
.

3.
Equality rights

Equality rights are guaranteed by
s-
s.15(1)
of the
Charter
:

15.(1)
Every individual is equal before and under the law and has the right to the
equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination and, in
particular, without discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin,
colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability.

Sub-section 15(1) provides that
every individual has the right to "equal benefit of the law without
discrimination".  One of the stated grounds of discrimination is
"religion".

Mr. Watson contends that it is
discrimination for Burnaby to confer on the Masons the right to use city lands
for the replica lodge when such a benefit is not accorded to the Protestant
Reformed Religion of which he is a member.

"Discrimination" as
recognized by s-
s.15(1)
of the
Charter
has been defined in
Andrews

v.
The Law Society of British Columbia
,

1989 CanLII 2 (SCC)
,
[1989] 1 S.C.R. 143
at 174-5
, per
McIntyre J. for the majority on this point:

"I
would say then that discrimination may be described as a distinction, whether
intentional or not but based on grounds relating to personal characteristics of
the individual or group, which has the effect of imposing burdens, obligations,
or disadvantages on such individual or group not imposed upon others, or which
withholds or limits access to opportunities, benefits, and advantages available
to other members of society."

This definition has become well
accepted in the jurisprudence of Canada:
R.
v.
Turpin
,
1989 CanLII 98 (SCC)
,
[1989] 1
S.C.R. 1296
at 1333
;
Haig
v.
Canada
,
1993 CanLII 58 (SCC)
,
[1993] 2 S.C.R. 995
at 1043
.
I emphasize the requirement that for a "distinction" to become
"discrimination" the distinction must be "based on grounds
relating to personal characteristics of the individual or group".

In this case there is neither
evidence nor fair inference that either Mr. Watson or the Christian Reformed
Religion have been denied any benefit based upon grounds of any of their
personal characteristics, including their religious beliefs.  What Burnaby has
done is approve a historical project on its merits.  The resolution does not
say or suggest that Burnaby will not consider other projects on their merits;
nor does it suggest that any proposals will be turned down on discriminatory
grounds.

I conclude therefore that the
resolution does not violate the rights of Mr. Watson or the Christian Reformed
Religion under s-
s.15(1)
of the
Charter
.

In case I am wrong in my analysis
of s-s.15(1) or its application to the facts of this case, I turn to a
consideration of whether the resolution may be saved under
s.1
of the
Charter
.

1.The

Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
guarantees the rights and
freedoms set out in it subject only to such reasonable limits prescribed by law
as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.

In my judgement the resolution
falls within the words "reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be
demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society".

In addressing s.1 justification
of an alleged violation of s-s.15(1), I propose to be guided by the approaches
stated by McIntyre and LaForest JJ.
in
Andrews
v.
Law Society of
British Columbia
, supra.  McIntyre J. said at pp.185-86:

"There
is no single test under s.1; rather, the Court must carefully engage in the
balancing of many factors in determining whether an infringement is reasonable
and demonstrably justified.

The
section 15(1) guarantee is the broadest of all guarantees. It applies to and
supports all other rights guaranteed by the
Charter
. However, it must be
recognized that Parliament and the Legislatures have a right and a duty to make
laws for the whole community; in this process, they must make innumerable
legislative distinctions and categorizations in the pursuit of the role of
government. When making distinctions between groups and individuals to achieve
desirable social goals, it will rarely be possible to say of any legislative
distinction that it is clearly the right legislative choice or that it is
clearly a wrong one. As stated by the Chief Justice in
R. v. Edwards Books
and Art Ltd
., at pp.781-82:

A
"reasonable limit" is one which, having regard to the principles
enunciated in
Oakes
, it was reasonable for the legislature to impose.
The courts are not called upon to substitute judicial opinions for legislative
ones as to the place at which to draw a precise line.

In
dealing with the many problems that arise legislatures must not be held to the
standard of perfection, for in such matters perfection is unattainable. I would
repeat the words of my colleague, LaForest J., in
R. v. Edwards Books and
Art Ltd
., at p.795:

By
the foregoing, I do not mean to suggest that this Court should, as a general
rule, defer to legislative judgments when those judgments trench upon rights
considered fundamental in a free and democratic society. Quite the contrary, I
would have thought the
Charter
established the opposite regime. On the
other hand, having accepted the importance of the legislative objective, one
must in the present context recognize that if the legislative goal is to be
achieved, it will inevitably be achieved to the detriment of some. Moreover,
attempts to protect the rights of one group will also inevitably impose burdens
on the rights of other groups.  There is no perfect scenario in which the
rights of all can be equally protected.

In
seeking to achieve a goal that is demonstrably justified in a free and
democratic society, therefore, a legislature must be given reasonable room to
manoeuvre to meet these conflicting pressures."

LaForest J. expressed general
agreement with the approach of McIntyre J.  He said, at pp.197-98:

"I
turn then to a consideration of the justifiability, fairness or proportionality
of the scheme. I agree with McIntyre J. that any such justification must be
found under
s.1
of the
Charter
, essentially because, in matters
involving infringements of fundamental rights, it is entirely appropriate that
government sustain the constitutionality of its conduct. I am in general agreement
with what he has to say about the manner in which legislation must be
approached under the latter provision, in particular the need for a
proportionality test involving a sensitive balancing of many factors in
weighing the legislative objective. If I have any qualifications to make, it is
that I prefer to think in terms of a single test for s.1, but one that is to be
applied to vastly differing situations with the flexibility and realism
inherent in the word "reasonable" mandated by the Constitution.

The
degree to which a free and democratic society such as Canada should tolerate
differentiation based on personal characteristics cannot be ascertained by an
easy calculus. There will rarely, if ever, be a perfect congruence between
means and ends, save where legislation has discriminatory purposes. The matter
must, as earlier cases have held, involve a test of proportionality. In cases
of this kind, the test must be approached in a flexible manner. The analysis
should be functional, focussing on the character of the classification in
question, the constitutional and societal importance to the individuals
affected of the benefit of which they are deprived, and the importance of the
state interest."

For the purposes of my analysis I
do not think there is any significant difference between the tests of McIntyre
J. and LaForest J.  The learned judges differed on the application of their
tests to the facts of the case before them (McIntyre J. dissented in result).
However, in my view they were in substantial accord on the tests they used.

In my opinion there is no doubt
that the preservation of our history, whether it be in books, museums,
monuments or classrooms, is a desirable social objective.  The achievement of
this goal, however, will inevitably involve choices upon which reasonable
people will differ.  What should be in a school curriculum?  Should old
churches, whether Roman Catholic or Protestant, be preserved as historic
sites?  Should a Jewish synagogue?  According to the analyses of McIntyre and
LaForest JJ.
in the
Andrews
case, law-makers must be accorded reasonable
scope to make decisions of this nature.

In this case the resolution
authorizing the replica lodge is for a desirable social objective
─
the re-creation of part of Burnaby's
history.  While Burnaby will supply the land and most of the maintenance costs,
the financial burden of constructing the replica lodge will be taken on by The
Gavel Historical Society.  So will the burden of supplying volunteers to operate
the building.  The building will become the property of Burnaby.  Under the
proposed agreement the Society will not be allowed use the building to promote
Masonry.  In all these circumstances I am of the view that the resolution is
both reasonable and proportional.

Accordingly I hold that the
resolution is justified by
s.1
of the
Charter
.

For the foregoing reasons I
reject ground No.3.

4.
Conflict of interest and
appearance of bias

Mr. Watson contends that
Councillor Young, being a Mason, should not have voted because he had a
personal interest in the outcome of the vote and there was a likelihood of bias
on his part.

Before the vote took place a Ms.
Rosabianca Starr, a property owner in Burnaby, asserted to Councillor Young
that because he was a Mason he was in a position of conflict of interest and
had an appearance of bias, and that he therefore ought not to vote.  Councillor
Young did not agree.  He seconded the motion to adopt the City Manager's
recommendation and voted for the motion.  The vote was 7
─
2 in favour.

There is no evidence to suggest
that Councillor Young had any financial interest in the outcome of the motion.
Nor is there any evidence to suggest he was a member of The Gavel Historical
Society.  The attack is solely based upon the fact he is a Mason.

The law relating to
disqualification of a councillor from voting because he or she has a personal
interest in the subject matter of the vote is found in both the common law and
the
Municipal Act
.

The common law is set out in the
leading case of
In Re L'Abbé and The Corporation of Blind River

(1904),

7 O.L.R. 230 (Div.Ct.)
per Boyd C., (Ferguson J. concurring) at pp.233-4:

"Now,
the interest or bias which disqualifies is one which exists separate and
distinct as to the individual in the particular case
─
not merely some interest possessed in
common with his fellows or the public generally: .... This may be a direct
monetary interest, or an interest capable of being measured pecuniarily, and in
such case that a bias exists in presumed. But there may be also substantial
interest other than pecuniary, and then the question arises, on all the
circumstances, as to whether there is a real likelihood of bias
─
a reasonable probability that the
interested person is likely to be biased with regard to the matter in
hand."

It is to be noted that the common law
covers both pecuniary and non-pecuniary interests as grounds for
disqualification from voting.  What will be a disqualifying interest will be a
question of fact in each case.  Boyd C. in the
L'Abbé
case put it this
way, at p.234:

"In
brief, it appears to be a question of fact in each instance of the
administration of public trusts to say whether the person voting in the
exercise of the trust has such a disqualifying interest as should estop him
from taking part and as should nullify his vote."

The common law was recently
restated in
Old St. Boniface Residents Association
v.
Winnipeg
,

1990 CanLII 31 (SCC)
,
[1990] 3 S.C.R. 1170
. Sopinka J. for the majority said by way of obiter dicta,
at p.1196:

"It
is not part of the job description that municipal councillors be personally
interested in matters that come before them beyond the interest that they have
in common with the other citizens in the municipality. Where such an interest
is found, both at common law and by statute, a member of Council is
disqualified if the interest is so related to the exercise of public duty that
a reasonably well-informed person would conclude that the interest might
influence the exercise of that duty. That is commonly referred to as a conflict
of interest."

The
Municipal Act
by a
1993 amendment (S.B.C. 1993, c.54, s.14) says that a councillor cannot vote on
matters in which he or she has a pecuniary interest.  The 1993 amendment
provides in part:

225. (7)Without
limiting subsection (4), a council member must not participate in the
discussion of or vote on a question in respect of a matter in which the member
has a direct or indirect pecuniary interest.

(8)Subsection
(7) does not apply

(a)if
the pecuniary interest of the council member is a pecuniary interest in common
with electors of the municipality generally,

(b)if
the matter relates to remuneration or expenses payable to one or more council
members in relation to their duties as council members, or

(c)if
the pecuniary interest is so remote or insignificant that it cannot reasonably
be regarded as likely to influence the member in relation to the matter.

Counsel for Burnaby submits that
as Councillor Young had no direct or indirect pecuniary interest in the subject
of the resolution he therefore should not be disqualified from voting.  She
relies upon the above-quoted provisions in the
Municipal Act
.  While it
is true that these provisions relate solely to pecuniary interest, in my
opinion the common law on interests other than pecuniary has not been displaced
by the putting into statutory form the substance of what was, before 1993, the
common law relating to pecuniary interest.  There is nothing in the 1993
amendment to indicate that the legislature intended a complete codification of
the law on disqualifying interests, nor to preclude the continued existence of
the common law relating to non-pecuniary interests.  See
Gendron
v.
Supply
and Services Union of The Public Service Alliance of Canada
,
1990 CanLII 110 (SCC)
,
[1990] 1
S.C.R. 1298
at 1315-16
;
Rawluk
v.
Rawluk
,
1990 CanLII 152 (SCC)
,
[1990] 1 S.C.R. 70
at
90
.

I return therefore to make some
observations on the
L'Abbé
and
Old St. Boniface
cases.  I draw
from
L'Abbé
that the non-pecuniary interest required to warrant
disqualification from voting must be a "substantial interest".  This,
I note, would eliminate interests that are remote or of little consequence.  I
draw from both
L'Abbé
and
Old St. Boniface
that the councillor's
interest in the subject matter of the vote must go beyond that which he or she
may have in common with other members of the community; it must be an interest
which is peculiar to the councillor, in effect, something that will serve his
or her own personal ends.  Finally, I draw from
Old St. Boniface
that
where there is such an interest it must be so related to the subject matter of
the vote that a reasonably well-informed person would conclude that the
interest may well influence the councillor's vote.

It is helpful to look at previous
cases to see where the courts have drawn the line between interests that
warrant councillors being disqualified from voting and interests that fall
short of requiring disqualification.  An example of an interest that
councillors have in common with the general community which will not disqualify
them from voting is the setting of tax rates which will, of course, have a
direct financial effect upon the councillors themselves:
Re McLean and The
Township of Ops
(1880), 45 U.C.Q.B. 325.  It is likewise where a by-law is
for the benefit of only a portion of the community and the councillor is a
member of that part of the community:
Elliott
v.
St. Catharines

(1908),
18 O.L.R. 57 (D.C.)
.  Meredith C.J. said at p.61:

"I
see no reason for differing from the view taken in the
McLean
case. As I
view it, the principle upon which the rule is founded is the same whether the
by-law is one affecting all the ratepayers of the municipality or only those
within a section of it."

The
L'Abbé
and
Elliott

cases were applied in
Re Blustein and Borough of North York
,
1967 CanLII 350 (ON HCJ)
,
[1967] 1
O.R. 604 (H.C.)
, where the court refused to disqualify a councillor from voting
on an amendment to North York's official plan which had the effect of bettering
the economic position of land held by a company in which the councillor was a
minority shareholder.  In arriving at its decision the court noted that the
real purpose of the amendment to the official plan was for the betterment of the
"economic, social and cultural" values of the inhabitants of the
area.  The decision was upheld by the Ontario Court of Appeal and leave to
appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada was refused:
1966 CanLII 517 (ON CA)
,
[1967] 1 O.R. 609
.

L'Abbé
,
McLean
,
Elliott

and
Blustein
were
cited in
Casson
v.
Reed
,
1975 CanLII 939 (AB SCAD)
,
[1975] 6 W.W.R.
431 (Alta. S.C. App. Div.)
.  The court held that a council member was
disentitled to vote on a motion to turn certain municipal lands into
recreational lands.  The councillor was disqualified because he was actively subdividing
and selling his own lands which were close by and would benefit from the
municipal lands becoming recreational.  The case is helpful in determining the
dividing line because  Clement J.A., for the court, observed (at pp.421-22)
that if the councillor had not been actively engaged in subdividing and selling
his land, he would not have been disqualified from voting.  He would simply
have had a community of interest with other land owners in the area benefitting
from the closeness of the proposed recreational complex.

In
Stewart
v.
City of
Yorkton

(1982),
1982 CanLII 2530 (SK QB)
,
18 M.P.L.R. 57 (Sask. Q.B.)
the court dealt with an
application to quash a by-law regulating the hours of opening of shops in
Yorkton.  It was alleged that two councillors were in positions of conflict of
interest.  One of the councillors was the local manager of Eaton's and the
other was a shareholder and officer of a shoe store.  Maurice J. applied
L'Abbé
,

Elliott
and
Casson
in concluding that the councillors' interests
were in common with all other owners and managers of stores in Yorkton.  He
ruled the councillors were entitled to vote on the by-law.

With these cases and principles
in mind, I now consider the situation of Councillor Young.  The resolution upon
which he voted

was for the purpose of erecting a
museum to re-create part of Burnaby's history.  The museum will be for the
benefit of all residents of Burnaby.  Councillor Young could expect no
pecuniary or other benefit from the replica of the 1914 Masonic Lodge.  There
is no evidence to suggest that he was or is a member of The Gavel Historical
Society.  He is, however, a Mason.

In my opinion, based upon the
facts of this case, Councillor Young is not in a conflict of interest
recognized by the common law.  He is not a member of The Gavel Historical
Society.  The project is essentially historical in nature, not religious.  The
replica building as part of the Burnaby Village Museum will be for the benefit
of all residents of Burnaby.  There are no personal ends to be gained by
Councillor Young over and above the benefits to his fellow citizens in Burnaby.

I test this reasoning by asking
myself what the situation would be if any councillors who were Christians voted
on a similar resolution to allow construction of a replica of an historic
Christian church at the Burnaby Village Museum.  Should they be precluded from
voting?  On comparable facts, my conclusion would be the same.

For the foregoing reasons I
reject this ground of attack on the resolution.

5.
Notice of the resolution

Mr. Watson alleges that one of
the opponents to the resolution, Ms. Rosabianca Starr, was promised by the City
Clerk that he would notify her of the meeting at which the resolution would be
voted upon and that he failed to do so.

The facts are critical to this
submission.

The City Manager's report first
came before Burnaby Council on February 23, 1994.  Ms. Starr and Mr. Watson
were in attendance at that council meeting.  It was moved and seconded that the
City Manager's recommendation be adopted.    Ms. Starr spoke with one of the
councillors and advised him that she wished an opportunity to speak against the
motion but that she was not prepared to do so that evening.  The motion was
then tabled by unanimous vote of the Council.

At the next City Council meeting,
held on March 7, 1994, a delegation which included Ms. Starr and Mr. Watson
requested an audience with the Council.  The Council unanimously passed a
resolution to hear the delegation.  Both Ms. Starr and Mr. Watson made presentations.
They spoke against the proposal to build a replica Masonic Lodge on city
property.  The Council decided not to lift the resolution from the table at
that time.  It was after this meeting when, according to Ms. Starr, the City
Clerk promised he would notify her of when further "action" was going
to be taken.  The City Clerk denies giving any such assurance.

The next meeting of City Council
was held March 14, 1994.  At this meeting the motion to approve the City
Manager's recommendations was lifted from the table (unanimously) and passed by
a 7
─
2 vote.
Ms. Starr says she was not notified by the City Clerk that this would be done.
The City Clerk, having denied giving any such undertaking to notify Ms. Starr
does not suggest that he did give her notice.

In my opinion, the factual
question of whether the City Clerk promised to notify Ms. Starr is without
significance because both Ms. Starr and Mr. Watson were in attendance at the
Council meeting and observed Council lifting the motion from the table and
voting upon the motion.

Council has the discretion to
allow interested persons to make presentations at Council meetings and this
opportunity was granted to Ms. Starr and Mr. Watson at Council's meeting of
March 7, 1994.  Both made presentations and their views were clearly made known
to Council.

Subject to any statutory
requirement to the contrary, a municipal council is not required to notify or
to grant a hearing to persons who may be affected by council's exercise of its
legislative powers:  Rogers,
The Law of Canadian Municipal Corporations

(2d) p.439, para.74.1;
Laurie's Caterers Ltd.
v.
North Vancouver

(1985),
1985 CanLII 496 (BC CA)
,
30 M.P.L.R. 145 (B.C.C.A.)
per Hutcheon J.A. in a concurring judgment
at 153;
Re Vancouver Charter; Re Wheatley

(1957),
1957 CanLII 669 (BC SC)
,
24 W.W.R. 323
(B.C.S.C.)
Clyne J. at 324.

No provision of the
Municipal
Act
was referred to me which either expressly or implicitly requires that
notice be provided to interested persons of Council's intention to pass a
resolution such as the one in this case.

On the facts of this case I
conclude that Mr. Watson and Ms. Starr were accorded more than their legal
rights.

I reject this ground of Mr.
Watson's submission.

Mr. Watson's right to claim a
Charter

remedy

Counsel for Burnaby drew the
court's attention to the fact that Mr. Watson is not a property taxpayer in
Burnaby.  He lives in his mother's house in Burnaby and she does pay property
taxes.  Counsel for Burnaby made it clear that she was not challenging Mr.
Watson's standing to bring this petition.  Her submission was that unless Mr.
Watson could show that his
Charter
rights have been violated, he is not
entitled to a
Charter
remedy.  It appears to me that this is a
self-evident proposition.  As Mr. Watson's
Charter
arguments have
failed, as have his submissions outside the
Charter
, if follows that he
must inevitably lose this petition.

Conclusion

Mr. Watson's petition is
dismissed with costs payable to Burnaby on level 3.

"D.W. Shaw, J."

Vancouver, B.C.

June 23, 1994
